def-het-ar1.title: First-order autoregressive errors
def-het-ar1.html: The errors follow a first-order autoregressive process, AR(1), if εt=ρεt−1+ut,t=2,…,n, with |ρ|<1, where u2,…,un are uncorrelated with mean zero and variance σu2, and the starting value ε1 has mean zero, variance σu2/(1−ρ2) and is uncorrelated with the ut.

def-het-dw.title: Durbin–Watson statistic
def-het-dw.html: For residuals ε^1,…,ε^n in time order, 𝛆𝛆𝛆𝛆d=∑t=2n(ε^t−ε^t−1)2∑t=1nε^t2=ε^⊤Aε^ε^⊤ε^,A=D⊤D, where D is the (n−1)×n first-difference matrix, with rows (…,0,−1,1,0,…).

def-het-hc.title: Heteroscedasticity-consistent covariance estimators
def-het-hc.html: Let ε^i and hii be the least squares residuals and leverages, with hii<1. For weights ωi, put V^ω=(X⊤X)−1(∑i=1nωix(i)x(i)⊤)(X⊤X)−1. The estimators HC0 to HC3 take ωi=ε^i2,nn−pε^i2,ε^i21−hii,ε^i2(1−hii)2.

eq-het-newey-west.html: Ω^L=∑k=−LL(1−|k|L+1)Γ^k,Γ^k=∑t=k+1nvtvt−k⊤,Γ^−k=Γ^k⊤,

eq-het-no-dominant-weight.html: maxici2‖c‖2→0.

eq-het-residual-second-moment.html: Eε^i2=(1−hii)2σi2+∑j≠imij2σj2.

eq-het-sandwich-true.html: 𝛃Cov(β^)=(X⊤X)−1(∑i=1nσi2x(i)x(i)⊤)(X⊤X)−1

eq-het-variance-function.html: 𝛂σi2=h(α0+zi⊤α),

eq-het-wls.html: 𝛃∑i=1nwi(yi−x(i)⊤b)2,soβ^W=(X⊤WX)−1X⊤Wy.

exm-het-ar1-coverage.title: Coverage with AR(1) errors
exm-het-ar1-coverage.html: Let the regressor be a fixed draw of an AR(1) series with coefficient 0.8, and the errors AR(1) with ρ=0.6 and normal innovations. Over 10,000 simulated data sets the nominal 95% intervals for the slope covered as follows. For n=50: least squares with the usual standard error 0.747, least squares with Newey–West 0.784, two-step Prais–Winsten 0.913, and generalized least squares with the true ρ 0.946. For n=200: 0.746, 0.871, 0.944 and 0.950. The Newey–West interval is valid only asymptotically, and converges slowly; when the AR(1) model is right, using it pays.

exm-het-ar1-efficiency.title: Three regressors
exm-het-ar1-efficiency.html:
Take n=100, an intercept, and one of three regressors: a linear trend, a fixed draw of white noise, and a fixed draw of an AR(1) series with coefficient 0.8 (its sample lag-one autocorrelation is 0.87). For AR(1) errors, Figure 21.6.1 shows (a) the ratio of the generalized to the ordinary least squares variance of the slope, and (b) the ratio of the true least squares variance to the expected nominal one, E(s2){(X⊤X)−1}22, with Es2 from @thm-rv-quadform-mean. All are exact computations.

At ρ=0.6: for the trend, least squares is 0.970 efficient but its nominal variance is too small by a factor of 4.01. For white noise it is only 0.462 efficient, yet its nominal variance is nearly right (factor 1.11). The autocorrelated regressor suffers both ways: efficiency 0.650, variance understated by a factor of 3.19. At ρ=0.9 the factors for the trend become 0.842 and 19.59.

The trend repeats the lesson of the autocorrelated-errors example of Section 19.2; the other two regressors are new.

exm-het-bp-size.title: Size of the two tests
exm-het-bp-size.html:
Take a straight-line regression with n=100 equally spaced values of x, constant variance, and zi=xi. In 40,000 simulated data sets the 5% tests rejected as follows:

error law κ Breusch–Pagan its limit Koenker
normal 3 0.048 0.050 0.050
Laplace 6 0.185 0.215 0.047
uniform 1.8 0.003 0.002 0.049

The Laplace law makes the Breusch–Pagan test reject nearly four times too often; the uniform law makes it almost never reject. The studentized test holds its level in all three cases.

exm-het-engel-fwls.title: Engel’s data, reweighted
exm-het-engel-fwls.html:
Regressing log⁡ε^i2 on an intercept and log⁡incomei gives slope γ^=1.90, so the fitted variance is proportional to income1.90, close to the square law suggested by Figure 21.2.1. Weighting by income−1.90 changes the slope from 0.4852 to 0.5711. The model-based standard error sw{(X⊤W^X)−1}221/2 of the weighted slope is 0.0149. The sandwich standard error of Section 21.4, which does not trust the variance model, is 0.0172 for the weighted slope and 0.0664 for the unweighted one. So weighting has cut the standard error by a factor of nearly four.

The variance function is not sharply determined by these data. Re-estimating γ from the residuals of the weighted fit, and repeating until it settles (10 iterations), moves γ^ to 2.52 and the slope to 0.5875, about one standard error away. Reporting the weighted estimate with the sandwich standard error protects against this uncertainty in the weights.

exm-het-engel-hc.title: Standard errors for Engel’s slope
exm-het-engel-hc.html: For the least squares slope of food expenditure on income, the classical standard error s{(X⊤X)−1}221/2 is 0.0144. The heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors are 0.0518 (HC0), 0.0520 (HC1), 0.0585 (HC2) and 0.0664 (HC3). The classical value is too small by a factor of 4.6 relative to HC3. Evidently the high-income households, which pin down the slope, are the noisy ones, so the classical formula, which averages the noise over all households, understates the uncertainty. The second listing above checks the jackknife identity of @prp-het-hc-facts(d).

exm-het-engel-leverage.title: One household carries the standard error
exm-het-engel-leverage.title_html: One household carries the standard error
exm-het-engel-leverage.html: In Engel’s data the household with the largest income has leverage 0.255. Its term ci2ε^i2/(1−hii)2 makes up 0.85 of the HC3 variance of the slope. The robust standard error of @exm-het-engel-hc is, in effect, an estimate of one household’s error variance. That is not a reason to go back to the classical standard error, which is far worse. It is a reason to look at that household (the influence measures of Chapter 20, such as @def-res-cooks, are the tools), to report how the conclusions change without it, and to prefer weighting, which here gives that household much less influence (@exm-het-engel-fwls).

exm-het-engel-plots.title: Engel’s food expenditure data
exm-het-engel-plots.html: Section 6.9 fitted Engel’s data on the annual income and food expenditure of 235 Belgian households, and noted that the spread of expenditure grows with income. The least squares slope is 0.4852. Figure 21.2.1 shows the residual plots. Panel (a) is a fan. Panel (b) plots |ri| against income on logarithmic scales. The slope of the fitted line, 0.96, suggests a standard deviation roughly proportional to income, the weighting used in @exm-proj-engel. The most extreme point, at the far right of panel (a), is the household with the largest income. Its leverage is 0.255, about thirty times the average p/n, and its residual is large and negative.

exm-het-engel-tests.title: Testing Engel’s data
exm-het-engel-tests.html: With zi=incomei, the Breusch–Pagan statistic is 636.0 and Koenker’s is 109.3, on one degree of freedom. Their ratio is 5.820=(κ^−1)/2, since the residuals have sample kurtosis 12.64. The heavy tails of the residuals inflate BP about sixfold, but the evidence is overwhelming either way: Koenker’s p-value is 1.4×10−25. White’s test, with income and its square, gives 181.1 on two degrees of freedom.

exm-het-hc-coverage.title: Coverage in a skewed design
exm-het-hc-coverage.html:
Let the regressor values be the n quantiles xi=exp⁡{Φ−1((i−1/2)/n)} of a standard lognormal distribution, a design with a long right tail like incomes. The largest leverage is 0.58 for n=25 and still 0.15 for n=1000. Figure 21.4.1 shows the coverage of nominal 95% intervals for the slope, with normal errors, over 20,000 simulated data sets for each n.

With constant variance (panel a) the classical interval is exact, and the robust intervals pay a price for their robustness: at n=25 they cover 0.852 (HC0), 0.866 (HC1), 0.895 (HC2) and 0.932 (HC3). With standard deviation proportional to x (panel b) the classical interval fails badly. Its coverage is 0.456 at n=25 and falls to 0.287 at n=1000, because the growing right tail of the design gives ever more influence to the noisiest observations. The robust intervals improve with n, but slowly. At n=25 they cover 0.631 (HC0), 0.650 (HC1), 0.760 (HC2) and 0.853 (HC3); at n=1000, 0.912, 0.912, 0.924 and 0.935. HC3 is the best of the four throughout, as Long and Ervin (2000) found in a wide range of designs.

exm-het-normal-plots.title: Three error laws
exm-het-normal-plots.html: Figure 21.1.1 shows plots for one simulated data set of n=60 observations with an intercept and two regressors (p=3), with three error laws of variance one. The normal case stays inside its envelope except for 3 scattered points, and the Shapiro–Wilk test described below gives p=0.519. Errors from a t(3) distribution give the S shape of heavy tails, with the largest residual far above the envelope (Shapiro–Wilk p<0.001). Centred exponential errors give a curved plot whose left end is too short and whose right end is too long (p=0.001).

exm-het-okun.title: A quarterly Okun’s-law regression
exm-het-okun.html: Okun’s law, named after the economist Arthur Okun, relates changes in unemployment to output growth. The statsmodels macroeconomic data give US quarterly series from 1959 to 2009. Regress the change in the unemployment rate (percentage points per quarter) on real GDP growth (percent, at an annual rate) for the n=202 quarters from the second quarter of 1959. The fitted line is Δu^t=0.227−0.0671gt, so unemployment is stable when output grows at about 0.227/0.0671≈3.4 percent a year, and each extra percentage point of growth lowers it by about 0.07 points per quarter. Figure 21.5.1(a,b) shows the residuals. They wander in long swings, and the lag plot tilts, with r1=0.300.

exm-het-okun-dw.title: The exact test for the Okun regression
exm-het-okun-dw.title_html: The exact test for the Okun regression
exm-het-okun-dw.html:
Under the hypothesis of independent normal errors, and given the growth series, d has mean 2.0031 and standard deviation 0.1399, and its 5% point is 1.773. The bounds for n=202, p=2 are dL,0.05=1.760 and dU,0.05=1.780, close together for a sample this large. The observed d=1.386 is far below both, and the exact one-sided p-value is 3.3×10−6.

The bounds matter in small samples. For the 40 quarters from the second quarter of 1999 to the first quarter of 2009, the same regression gives d=1.478, between the bounds 1.442 and 1.544: the bounds test is inconclusive. The exact p-value, 0.037, settles it. Figure 21.5.1(c) shows the three null densities for this window.

exm-het-okun-dynamic.title: Okun’s law, dynamically
exm-het-okun-dynamic.html: Regressing Δut on an intercept, Δut−1, gt and gt−1 gives coefficients 0.2160, 0.3571 (standard error 0.0574), −0.0487 (0.0043) and −0.0162 (0.0055). The AR(1) model would require the last coefficient to be −0.3571×(−0.0487)=0.0174. The estimate has the opposite sign, and the delta-method test of the restriction gives z=−8.1. The unrestricted dynamic regression has no remaining residual autocorrelation: its Breusch–Godfrey statistic with four lags is 4.42, with p-value 0.35. Unemployment responds to growth with a lag and with persistence; the AR(1) error model mistook this for correlated noise, and the slope estimates of @exm-het-okun-pw, which move with ρ^, were artefacts of that mistake.

exm-het-okun-pw.title: Okun’s law with AR(1) errors
exm-het-okun-pw.html: For the regression of @exm-het-okun, ρ^=0.303. The two-step Prais–Winsten estimate of the slope is −0.0506 with standard error 0.0049, against the least squares −0.0671 with nominal standard error 0.0050. Iterating Cochrane–Orcutt to convergence takes 17 iterations and ends at ρ^=0.548 and slope −0.0380. The estimate of the effect of growth on unemployment thus changes by almost half depending on the treatment of the errors, and the residuals of the transformed regression still have lag-one autocorrelation 0.148. Both facts suggest that the AR(1) error model does not describe these data. We return to this below.

exm-het-replicates.title: Weights from a few replicates
exm-het-replicates.html: Take ten design points x=1,…,10, m replicates at each, a straight-line mean, and normal errors with standard deviation proportional to x. Figure 21.3.1 compares four slope estimates by their variance relative to weighted least squares with the true weights. Ordinary least squares has 2.44 times the optimal variance when m=2, and about the same for every m. Weights 1/sg2 from the within-group sample variances are a disaster for small groups: with m=2 their variance is 5.44 times the optimum, twice that of the unweighted fit, and with m=3 it is still 2.67, worse than no weighting. They approach the optimum only slowly (1.22 for m=10, 1.05 for m=30). Worse, the model-based interval, which treats the estimated weights as known, covers the true slope in only 0.47 of the data sets for m=2, 0.65 for m=3 and 0.80 for m=5. Weights from a fitted variance function, the regression of log⁡sg2 on log⁡xg, are far better: 1.41 times the optimum for m=2, 1.12 for m=3 and 1.04 for m=5.

exm-het-supernormality.title: How much nonnormality survives
exm-het-supernormality.html: Take n=30 observations, an intercept, and p−1 columns of standard normal regressors. Averaged over the observations, the share of the errors’ excess kurtosis that survives in the standardized residuals is 0.873 for p=2, 0.467 for p=10 and 0.162 for p=20. The share of skewness is 0.898, 0.532 and 0.162. With centred exponential errors (skewness 2, excess kurtosis 6) and p=10, the residual with the largest leverage, hii=0.57, has predicted excess kurtosis 1.23, against 1.26 in 200,000 simulated data sets. For the ordered values, the average squared distance between sorted residuals and sorted errors was 0.133, while the bound in (b) averaged 0.330, close to its expectation p/n=1/3.

exm-het-sw-power.title: Power lost to supernormality
exm-het-sw-power.html: In the same designs (n=30), the 5% Shapiro–Wilk test applied to the unobservable centred exponential errors rejects in 0.96 to 0.97 of simulated data sets. Applied to the residuals it rejects in 0.92 for p=2, 0.45 for p=10 and only 0.07 for p=20. For errors from t(5), rescaled to variance one, the rates are 0.24 to 0.25 for the errors and 0.23, 0.14 and 0.05 for the residuals.

exr-het-ar1-inflation.title: B2
exr-het-ar1-inflation.html: Let the regressor be a stationary AR(1) series with coefficient ϕ, independent of AR(1) errors with coefficient ρ. Show heuristically that the ratio of the true variance of the least squares slope to its nominal variance tends to (1+ρϕ)/(1−ρϕ).

exr-het-ar1-inverse.title: A1
exr-het-ar1-inverse.html: Compute Lρ⊤Lρ and show that it is tridiagonal with diagonal (1,1+ρ2,…,1+ρ2,1) and off-diagonal entries −ρ. Check VρLρ⊤Lρ=I for n=2.

exr-het-ar1-white.title: B1
exr-het-ar1-white.html: Let the regressor xt be white noise with variance τ2, independent of AR(1) errors, and consider the slope in a regression through the origin. Show heuristically that nVar(β^OLS)→σu2/{(1−ρ2)τ2} and nVar(β^GLS)→σu2/{(1+ρ2)τ2}, so that the efficiency of least squares, the ratio bounded in @thm-dep-efficiency, tends to (1−ρ2)/(1+ρ2).

exr-het-averages.title: A2
exr-het-averages.html: A laboratory reports only the mean y¯i of mi replicate measurements at each of k settings x(i), where the individual measurements have common variance σ2. Which weights should be used? What does sw2 then estimate, and why is it not the replicate variance σ2 unless the model for the means is correct?

exr-het-co-first.title: B3
exr-het-co-first.html: In the model yt=α+βt+εt, t=1,…,n, with AR(1) errors, show that the Cochrane–Orcutt regression has columns (1−ρ)1 and (1−ρ)t+ρ on t=2,…,n, and that the information it carries about β is (1−ρ)2∑t≥2(t−t¯)2/σu2, where t¯ is the mean of 2,…,n. What happens as ρ→1 with n fixed, and why does the Prais–Winsten first row change the picture?

exr-het-duplicated-rows.title: B2
exr-het-duplicated-rows.html: Some programs implement integer weights wi by repeating row i of the data wi times and running ordinary least squares. Show that this gives the correct 𝛃β^W but divides the weighted residual sum of squares by ∑iwi−p instead of n−p. Which standard errors are then wrong, and in which direction?

exr-het-dw-alternative.title: B1
exr-het-dw-alternative.html: If 𝛆Cov(ε)=σ2V, show that 𝛆𝛆E(ε^⊤Aε^)=σ2tr{A(I−M)V(I−M)}. For n=3, X=1 and vst=ρ|s−t|, compute it and show that it decreases in ρ.

exr-het-dw-asymptotic.title: C1
exr-het-dw-asymptotic.html: For the intercept-only model, show that under the hypothesis Vard=4(n−2)/{(n−1)(n+1)} exactly, so that the standard deviation of d is close to 2/n. (Use @thm-het-durbin-watson(b), ∑jλj2=tr(A2), and the entries of A.) Compare with the Okun regression of @exm-het-okun-dw.

exr-het-dw-bounds-attained.title: B2
exr-het-dw-bounds-attained.html: Suppose C(X) is spanned by the eigenvectors v1,…,vp of A. Show that νk=λk+p for all k, so that d=dU. Which columns of X have this property, and what do they look like?

exr-het-dw-intercept.title: A2
exr-het-dw-intercept.html: For the intercept-only model X=1, show that Ed=2 exactly under the hypothesis.

exr-het-dw-invariance.title: B3
exr-het-dw-invariance.html: Show that d is unchanged if y is replaced by cy+Xa for any c≠0 and a. Use this to explain why its null distribution cannot depend on 𝛃β or σ, without appeal to normality.

exr-het-dw-lagged.title: C2
exr-het-dw-lagged.html: In the model yt=βyt−1+εt with independent errors, fitted by least squares on t=2,…,n, argue that the residuals are less autocorrelated than the errors would be under an autocorrelated alternative, so that d is biased towards 2. Relate this to the requirement in @thm-het-durbin-watson that X be fixed.

exr-het-dw-range.title: A1
exr-het-dw-range.html: Show that 0≤d<4 and that d=2(1−r1)−(ε^12+ε^n2)/∑tε^t2. Which residual patterns give values near 0 and near 4?

exr-het-ecdf.title: C1
exr-het-ecdf.html: Under the assumptions of @prp-het-normal-check, suppose p/n→0 along a sequence of designs. Let F^n and Fn be the empirical distribution functions of the residuals and of the errors. Show that F^n(x)−Fn(x)→0 in probability at every continuity point x of F.

exr-het-envelope-free.title: B1
exr-het-envelope-free.html: Assume 𝛃Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I). Show that the internally and externally studentized residuals are functions of 𝛆𝛆g=ε^/‖ε^‖, and that the law of g does not depend on 𝛃β or σ. Conclude that the simulated envelope of this section is exact, whatever 𝛃β and σ are used in the simulation.

exr-het-exponential-coverage.title: B2
exr-het-exponential-coverage.html: For centred exponential errors, ε=E−1 with E standard exponential, show that the limit in @prp-ci-pi-limit at the 95% level is 1−e−2.96, and find the probabilities of missing below and above.

exr-het-fitted-weights.title: B3
exr-het-fitted-weights.html: Weights w^i=|Y^i|−2θ depend on the fitted values. Show that they are not functions of 𝛆ε^ alone, and find where the symmetry argument of @thm-het-wls(c) fails. What happens for a single regressor through the origin, Yi=βxi+εi with every xi≠0?

exr-het-gq-ordering.title: B2
exr-het-gq-ordering.html: Under the assumptions of @prp-het-goldfeld-quandt, suppose the observations are sorted by their fitted values Y^i instead of by a fixed variable. Show that FGQ still has the F(n2−p,n1−p) distribution. Show by an example that sorting by |ε^i| destroys the result.

exr-het-hac-hc0.title: A2
exr-het-hac-hc0.html: Show that the Newey–West estimator with L=0 is HC0, and that with X=1 and L≥1 it estimates the long-run variance ∑kγk of a stationary series, scaled by n.

exr-het-hac-negative.title: C1
exr-het-hac-negative.html: Give vectors v1,v2,v3 (with p=1) for which the unweighted sum ∑|k|≤1Γ^k is negative.

exr-het-hc-homoscedastic-bias.title: B1
exr-het-hc-homoscedastic-bias.html: In simple regression with an intercept and constant variance, show that the relative bias of HC0 for the slope variance is −∑i(xi−x¯)2hii/Sxx. Evaluate it for x=(1,2,3,4,10) of @exr-het-residual-variance.

exr-het-hc-jackknife-centred.title: C2
exr-het-hc-jackknife-centred.html: The usual jackknife variance is 𝛃𝛃n−1n∑i(β^(i)−m)(β^(i)−m)⊤, where m is the mean of the 𝛃β^(i). Express it in terms of V^HC3 and the vector ∑ix(i)ε^i/(1−hii), and show that the two agree to first order when maxihii→0.

exr-het-hc-random.title: C1
exr-het-hc-random.html: Suppose the rows (x(i),εi) are independent copies of a random pair with E(ε∣x)=0, E‖x‖4<∞, Eε4<∞ and Exx⊤ positive definite. Adapt the proof of @thm-het-sandwich to show that HC0 is consistent in the sense of part (a), replacing Chebyshev’s inequality by the weak law of large numbers.

exr-het-hc-wls.title: B2
exr-het-hc-wls.html: Using @thm-het-wls(b), write down a sandwich estimator of the covariance of a weighted least squares estimate with fixed weights W, and show that it reduces to HC0 applied to the rescaled data (W1/2X,W1/2y).

exr-het-inverse-chisq.title: C1
exr-het-inverse-chisq.html: Show that E(1/U)=∞ if U∼χ2(1), and that E(1/U)=1/(k−2) if U∼χ2(k) with k≥3. Explain what this implies for weights 1/sg2 computed from m replicates.

exr-het-levene.title: C1
exr-het-levene.html: Suppose the observations fall into g groups and zi consists of g−1 group indicators. Show that Koenker’s statistic is n times the R2 of a one-way analysis of variance of the squared residuals, and compare it with Levene’s test.

exr-het-leverage-one.title: A2
exr-het-leverage-one.html: What happens to HC0, HC2 and HC3 if some observation has hii=1? Explain why no estimator built from residuals can estimate that observation’s contribution to 𝛌𝛃Var(λ⊤β^).

exr-het-oneway-kurtosis.title: B3
exr-het-oneway-kurtosis.html: In a one-way layout in which every group has m observations, show that the kurtosis factor of @prp-het-normal-check(c) is the same for every residual and equals b=(1−1/m)4+(m−1)/m4(1−1/m)2. Evaluate it for m=2 and m=5, and explain why residual plots from small groups say little about the tails of the errors.

exr-het-origin-efficiency.title: B1
exr-het-origin-efficiency.html: In the model yi=βxi+εi with xi>0 and Var(εi)=σ2xi2, show that the weighted estimate is the mean of the ratios yi/xi, and that the efficiency of ordinary least squares relative to it is (∑ixi2)2/(n∑ixi4)≤1. Evaluate the efficiency for x=1,…,10.

exr-het-random-coefficients.title: B1
exr-het-random-coefficients.html: Let 𝛃yi=x(i)⊤(β+ui)+εi, where ui has mean 0 and covariance Ω, εi has variance σ2, and all are independent. Show that Var(yi) is a linear function of the squares and cross products of the regressors. Which test of this section is the score-type test for Ω=0?

exr-het-residual-moment.title: A1
exr-het-residual-moment.html: Derive @eq-het-residual-second-moment. Show that under constant variance Eε^i2=σ2(1−hii), and give an example in which σi2 is the largest variance but Eε^i2 is the smallest.

exr-het-residual-variance.title: A1
exr-het-residual-variance.html: In simple regression with n=5 and x=(1,2,3,4,10), compute the leverages and the variances of the five residuals when σ2=1. Which residual is least like its error, in the sense of @prp-het-normal-check(a)?

exr-het-welch.title: A1
exr-het-welch.html: Take the two-group model ygj=μg+εgj, g=1,2, j=1,…,ng. Show that HC2 for μ^1−μ^2 equals s12/n1+s22/n2, the variance estimate of Welch’s test, where sg2 is the sample variance of group g. What does HC0 give?

exr-het-white-test.title: B3
exr-het-white-test.html: White’s test compares s2X⊤X with ∑iε^i2x(i)x(i)⊤. Show that the difference of these matrices, divided by n, has entries n−1∑i(ε^i2−s2)xijxik, and explain why Koenker’s statistic with zi the distinct products xijxik tests whether these are jointly zero.

exr-het-wls-residuals.title: A1
exr-het-wls-residuals.html: Under @thm-het-wls(a), show that 𝛃E∑iwi(Yi−x(i)⊤β^W)2=σ2(n−p), and that the raw residual 𝛃Yi−x(i)⊤β^W has variance σ2(1−gii)/wi, where gii is the ith leverage of the weighted fit.

lem-het-clt.title: A central limit theorem for weighted sums
lem-het-clt.title_html: A central limit theorem for weighted sums
lem-het-clt.html:
For each n let ξ1,…,ξn be independent with mean zero, and let c=cn∈Rn be nonzero weights with maxici2‖c‖2→0.{#eq-het-no-dominant-weight}

Suppose either (a) the ξi have a common distribution, not depending on n, with variance τ2∈(0,∞), or (b) for some constants δ,K,τmin>0, Varξi≥τmin2 and E|ξi|2+δ≤K for all i and n. Then ∑iciξi(∑ici2Varξi)1/2→N(0,1)in distribution.

lem-het-dw-eigen.title: Eigenvalues of the difference matrix
lem-het-dw-eigen.html: The eigenvalues of A are λj=4sin2⁡(π(j−1)2n),j=1,…,n, with eigenvectors vj=(cos⁡(θj/2),cos⁡(3θj/2),…,cos⁡((2n−1)θj/2))⊤, where θj=π(j−1)/n. In particular 0=λ1<λ2<⋯<λn<4, and v1=1.

lem-het-interlace.title: Interlacing
lem-het-interlace.html: Let B be N×N symmetric with eigenvalues β1≤⋯≤βN, and let U be N×m with orthonormal columns. If μ1≤⋯≤μm are the eigenvalues of U⊤BU, then βk≤μk≤βk+N−m for k=1,…,m.

prp-het-goldfeld-quandt.title: Goldfeld–Quandt
prp-het-goldfeld-quandt.html: Let 𝛃Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I), let the two groups be chosen without reference to Y, and let X1 and X2, their rows of X, have rank p<nk. If SSE1 and SSE2 are the residual sums of squares of the separate fits, then FGQ=SSE2/(n2−p)SSE1/(n1−p)∼F(n2−p, n1−p).

prp-het-hc-facts.title: Finite-sample properties
prp-het-hc-facts.html:
Let 𝛌λ∈Rp and 𝛌c=X(X⊤X)−1λ, so that 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃𝛆λ⊤β^−λ⊤β=c⊤ε and 𝛌𝛌λ⊤V^ωλ=∑ici2ωi.

  1. Under constant variance σ2, 𝛌𝛌𝛌𝛃E(λ⊤V^HC2λ)=Var(λ⊤β^), while 𝛌𝛌𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃E(λ⊤V^HC0λ)=Var(λ⊤β^)−σ2∑ici2hii≤Var(λ⊤β^) and 𝛌𝛌𝛌𝛃E(λ⊤V^HC3λ)≥Var(λ⊤β^).

  2. In general, 𝛌𝛌E(λ⊤V^HC0λ)=∑ici2∑j(I−M)ij2σj2.

  3. V^HC0⪯V^HC2⪯V^HC3 in the order of nonnegative definiteness.

  4. 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃V^HC3=∑i=1n(β^(i)−β^)(β^(i)−β^)⊤, where 𝛃β^(i) is the estimate with observation i deleted.

prp-het-newey-west.title: Newey–West estimates are nonnegative definite
prp-het-newey-west.html: For any vectors v1,…,vn and any L≥0, Ω^L in @eq-het-newey-west is nonnegative definite. Without the weights, ∑|k|≤LΓ^k need not be.

prp-het-normal-check.title: What residuals reveal about the errors
prp-het-normal-check.title_html: What residuals reveal about the errors
prp-het-normal-check.html:
Let ε1,…,εn be independent and identically distributed with mean 0 and variance σ2, and let rank(X)=p.

  1. 𝛆ε^i−εi=−(Mε)i, which has mean 0 and variance σ2hii. The total 𝛆𝛆E‖ε^−ε‖2 equals σ2p.

  2. Let ε^(1)≤⋯≤ε^(n) and ε(1)≤⋯≤ε(n) be the ordered residuals and ordered errors. Then 𝛆1n∑i=1n(ε^(i)−ε(i))2≤1n‖Mε‖2, and the right-hand side has expectation σ2p/n.

  3. Suppose the errors have skewness γ1=Eε3/σ3 and excess kurtosis γ2=Eε4/σ4−3. If hii<1, the standardized residual ε^i/(σ1−hii) has skewness aiγ1 and excess kurtosis biγ2, where ai=∑jcij3(1−hii)3/2,bi=∑jcij4(1−hii)2, with |ai|≤1 and (1−hii)2≤bi≤1.

thm-het-ar1.title: Regression with AR(1) errors
thm-het-ar1.html:
Let 𝛃𝛆Y=Xβ+ε with rank(X)=p and AR(1) errors.

  1. Cov(εs,εt)=σu2ρ|s−t|/(1−ρ2). Write 𝛆Cov(ε)=σu2Vρ.

  2. (Prais–Winsten transformation.) Let Lρ be the n×n lower bidiagonal matrix with (Lρ)11=1−ρ2, (Lρ)tt=1 and (Lρ)t,t−1=−ρ for t≥2. Then 𝛆Cov(Lρε)=σu2I, so Vρ−1=Lρ⊤Lρ and detVρ=1/(1−ρ2). For known ρ, the generalized least squares estimate is ordinary least squares on (Lρy,LρX), and it is the best linear unbiased estimator.

  3. (Likelihood.) If the errors are normal, the log-likelihood is 𝛃𝛃ℓ(β,ρ,σu2)=−n2log⁡(2πσu2)+12log⁡(1−ρ2)−‖Lρ(y−Xβ)‖22σu2.

  4. (Cochrane–Orcutt.) Let 𝛃𝛃S(β,ρ)=∑t=2n{(yt−ρyt−1)−(x(t)−ρx(t−1))⊤β}2, the sum of squares of the last n−1 rows of 𝛃Lρ(y−Xβ). Alternate the steps 𝛃𝛃ρk+1=∑t≥2etet−1∑t≥2et−12  with e=y−Xβk,βk+1=argminbS(b,ρk+1). Then 𝛃𝛃𝛃S(βk+1,ρk+1)≤S(βk,ρk+1)≤S(βk,ρk), so S decreases along the iterations, and any limit point 𝛃(β∗,ρ∗) with |ρ∗|<1 at which the steps are continuous is a stationary point of S.

thm-het-breusch-pagan.title: Breusch–Pagan and Koenker
thm-het-breusch-pagan.html:
Let Z~ have full column rank q.

  1. (Score statistic.) Suppose εi∼N(0,σi2) independently, with @eq-het-variance-function, h continuously differentiable, and h′≠0 at the null value of α0. The score statistic for 𝛂α=0 is BP=12(u−1)⊤Z~(Z~⊤Z~)−1Z~⊤(u−1), half the explained sum of squares from regressing ui on an intercept and zi. It does not depend on h.

  2. (Studentized form.) Let K=nR2. Then BP=12(κ^−1)K.

  3. (Null distributions.) Suppose instead only that the errors are independent and identically distributed with mean 0, variance σ2, finite fourth moment μ4 and kurtosis κ=μ4/σ4>1, that rank(X)=p and q are fixed, that the zi are bounded, and that n−1Z~⊤Z~→Qz, positive definite. Then, as n→∞, K→χ2(q),BP→12(κ−1)χ2(q)in distribution.

thm-het-durbin-watson.title: Durbin–Watson
thm-het-durbin-watson.html:
Let 𝛃Y∼Nn(Xβ,σ2I) with rank(X)=p<n, let the columns of the n×(n−p) matrix Q⊥ be an orthonormal basis of C(X)⊥, and let ν1≤⋯≤νn−p be the eigenvalues of Q⊥⊤AQ⊥. Put m=n−p.

  1. d has the distribution of ∑kνkξk2/∑kξk2, where ξ1,…,ξm are independent N(0,1). It depends on X but not on 𝛃β or σ2, and d is independent of 𝛆𝛆SSE=ε^⊤ε^.

  2. Ed=ν¯=m−1∑kνk=tr{(I−M)A}/m and Vard=2∑k(νk−ν¯)2m(m+2).

  3. Pr(d≤c)=Pr{∑k(νk−c)ξk2≤0} for every c.

  4. (Bounds.) If 1∈C(X), then λk+1≤νk≤λk+p for k=1,…,m, with λj as in @lem-het-dw-eigen. Consequently dL≤d≤dU with probability one, where, for the same ξk, dL=∑kλk+1ξk2∑kξk2,dU=∑kλk+pξk2∑kξk2, whose distributions depend only on n and p.

thm-het-sandwich.title: Consistency of the sandwich estimators
thm-het-sandwich.html:
Let 𝛃𝛆Y=Xβ+ε with p fixed. Assume that

  • (H1) the errors are independent with mean zero and variances σi2, with σi2≥σmin2>0 and Eεi4≤K for all i;
  • (H2) the rows satisfy ‖x(i)‖≤C for all i;
  • (H3) n−1X⊤X→A, a positive definite matrix.

Let V^ be any of HC0–HC3, and 𝛃V=Cov(β^) as in @eq-het-sandwich-true. Then:

  1. n(V^−V)→0 in probability;

  2. for every fixed 𝛌λ≠0, 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛌(λ⊤β^−λ⊤β)/(λ⊤V^λ)1/2→N(0,1) in distribution;

  3. for every fixed p×q matrix Λ of rank q, 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃W=(Λ⊤β^−Λ⊤β)⊤(Λ⊤V^Λ)−1(Λ⊤β^−Λ⊤β) tends to χ2(q) in distribution.

thm-het-wls.title: Weighted least squares with known and estimated weights
thm-het-wls.title_html: Weighted least squares with known and estimated weights
thm-het-wls.html:
Let 𝛃𝛆Y=Xβ+ε with 𝛆Eε=0 and rank(X)=p.

  1. (Known weights.) If 𝛆Cov(ε)=σ2W−1 with W known, then 𝛃β^W is the best linear unbiased estimator of 𝛃β, 𝛃Cov(β^W)=σ2(X⊤WX)−1 and Esw2=σ2. If 𝛆ε is normal, 𝛃𝛃β^W∼Np(β,σ2(X⊤WX)−1) independently of (n−p)sw2/σ2∼χ2(n−p).

  2. (Wrong weights.) If 𝛆Cov(ε)=Σ is arbitrary and W is any fixed positive diagonal matrix, then 𝛃β^W is unbiased with 𝛃Cov(β^W)=(X⊤WX)−1X⊤WΣWX(X⊤WX)−1.

  3. (Estimated weights, symmetric errors.) Let 𝛆W^=W(ε^) be a positive diagonal matrix that depends on the data only through the ordinary least squares residuals, with W(−e)=W(e). If 𝛆−ε has the same distribution as 𝛆ε and 𝛃E‖β^W^‖<∞, then 𝛃𝛃Eβ^W^=β.

  4. (Estimated weights from groups.) Suppose the observations form G groups, fixed in advance, that the errors are independent, and that within group g they are identically distributed with variance σg2>0. Let ng→∞ for each g with n−1Xg⊤Xg→Ag, where Xg holds the rows of group g, and let Aw=∑gAg/σg2 be positive definite. Let W have entries 1/σg2, and W^ have entries 1/σ^g2, where 𝛆σ^g2=‖ε^g‖2/ng is the mean squared ordinary least squares residual in group g. Then 𝛃𝛃n(β^W^−β^W)→0andn(X⊤W^X)−1→Aw−1 in probability, while 𝛃nCov(β^W)=n(X⊤WX)−1→Aw−1.
